entries.title: ‘Is there any value in writing a story in a time of chaos?’: novelist Elif Shafak on her creative crisis
entries.summary: The author talks about her nomadic childhood, being targeted by the Turkish government and overcoming depression to write her latest novelFor a long time Elif Shafak was referred to as Turkey’s “most widely read female author”. Today, she is surely simply its best loved. Orhan Pamuk may have won the Nobel prize in literature, but it is Shafak whose novels are fervently passed among readers. There
entries.content:
For a long time Elif Shafak was referred to as Turkey’s “most widely read female author”. Today, she is surely simply its best loved. Orhan Pamuk may have won the Nobel prize in literature, but it is Shafak whose novels are fervently passed among readers. There Are Rivers in the Sky, which follows a single raindrop from ancient Nineveh to the River Tigris in 2018, was one of the UK’s bestselling literary novels last year. The Island of Missing Trees, a love story set in post-colonial Cyprus and contemporary London, was shortlisted for the Women’s prize in 2022, and 10 Minutes 38 seconds in This Strange World, narrated by a murdered sex worker in Istanbul, was shortlisted for the Booker prize in 2019. Last December she was elected president of the Royal Society of Literature. It would be tempting to say she is on a roll, but Shafak’s reputation and readership have been steadily growing for more than 20 years and spanning as many books, of which 14 are novels.

In a 2017 Ted Talk, which has been viewed more than 6.4m times, she describes herself as an Istanbulite, “a European by birth and by choice” and a Londoner for many years. “I like to think of myself as a global soul, as a world citizen, a nomad and an itinerant storyteller.” Her novels sweep confidently across centuries and continents, taking in politics, history, feminism and ecology, typically with a dash of magic realism or mysticism.

Her latest, In One Brief Moment All Eternity, is a stylistically inventive fictionalised life of Gustave Flaubert. “This book is really my love letter to literature,” Shafak says over coffee in west London, where the 54-year-old author has lived with her husband and two children for the past 18 years. While Flaubert is now considered the godfather of the modern novel – as Nabokov said, without Flaubert there would have been no Marcel Proust or James Joyce – most of his life was spent toiling in obscurity. It is this that interests Shafak. “The book is about a lonely boy who was misunderstood by almost everyone around him, including his own family members. He was regarded as a failure, as a disappointment, treated as ‘the other’.” The novel is dedicated to anyone who may have felt similarly treated. “I wanted to be able to say, ‘you’re my brother, you’re my sister’. That was the beginning,” she says.

Shafak talks with the same fluency and lyrical intensity as she writes, in long, far-reaching sentences. In person, she also listens intently and smiles often, despite the seriousness of her words. We last met when she was part of the panel to discuss the Guardian’s 100 best novels of all time list earlier this year: Madame Bovary was in her top 10, but, like Flaubert himself, she is a huge fan of Don Quixote. On stage, she had the softest voice, but when she speaks, everyone listens. She has recently enjoyed renewed popularity with younger readers on BookTok. It is no wonder there are snaking queues of readers of all ages and nationalities for the signings after her literary events.

In One Brief Moment All Eternity arose out of our own historical moment, which Shafak has dubbed “The age of three As: Angst, Anger and AI”. Yet it also started from “a very personal place”, she says, when she was struggling with depression and anxiety, or hüzün in Turkish, meaning a deep melancholy. “In the middle of a world shaped by wars and violence, division, climate crisis, technological uncertainties, you find yourself asking, ‘What is the meaning of shutting yourself in a small room and worrying about the perfect synonym?’” she says. “Is there any value in writing a short story, a poem, a novel in a time of crisis and chaos, such as the one we’re going through? I wanted to take a closer look at this question – creativity in a time of crisis.”

This led her back to the 19th century, another era of change and confusion, in which “there lived a beloved novelist who dedicated his entire life to literature in a very passionate way”. While Flaubert set out to inhabit the female mind – then a radical proposition for a male novelist – Shafak upends the premise of Madame Bovary to tell his story through multiple women whose paths may have crossed with his. “I wanted to bring together the European canon of the novel with the Middle Eastern oral tradition of storytelling,” she explains. “You open a box and inside there’s another box, under this story, there’s another story. There’s a polyphony of voices.”

And so Flaubert’s life is told not just through the eyes of his beloved nursemaid, Julie; his maman; his long-term mistress, Louise Colet; and his confidant George Sand, but also an acrobat he encounters as a boy, a camel called Jamilah and Emma Bovary herself. We meet an Egyptian dancer and courtesan, Kuchuck Hanem, with whom Flaubert becomes enraptured on his travels in the Middle East, passingly mentioned in biographies. “I wanted to remember this woman and say, ‘Maybe this is the woman who inspired Madame Bovary,’” Shafak says. “I want to claim that at the heart of this iconic French European literary heroine, there is an Egyptian belly dancer.” Opium, syphilis and Istanbul (Shafak always thinks of the city as “she”) are also given their own chapters.

“Every time I start writing a book, I say to myself, ‘This time I’m going to keep it minimalist,’” she laughs. “I think because of who I am, my upbringing, all these cultural influences are like tributaries that flow into it. We are all interconnected, not only with each other as fellow human beings, but with nature. For me, the long narrative form is about honouring those connections.”

They may be separated by nearly two centuries, by nationality and by gender, but once she started looking, the connections between Flaubert’s story and her own were striking, “starting with that lonely childhood, with that feeling of being the other,” she says.

Although her parents were Turkish, Shafak was born in Strasbourg, France, in 1971, where her father was studying for a PhD. Her parents divorced five years later and the young Elif and her mother returned to live with her maternal grandmother in Ankara. Like Flaubert, Shafak grew up with two maternal figures. Although her grandmother was uneducated, she insisted her mother return to university, which she had left when she married. Shafak called her mother “big sister”, her grandmother “mother”: “From one I got my love for written culture, from the other I got my love for oral storytelling,” she says. She remembers her grandmother’s flat as a place full of magic, lefty students and Gauloises cigarette smoke.

For all the love in her childhood, Shafak felt abandoned by her father, an academic who remarried. Like the celebrated Doctor Flaubert, Gustave’s father, he was “very detached, very aloof”. She didn’t see him for most of her childhood, and for a long time was very angry that he was such a good father to her half-brothers. “I felt like I was the forgotten child. There was a void. There was an absence of love,” she says. “And I think absences also shape us. Silences also shape us.”

After she finally graduated, her mother became a teacher and then a diplomat. When Shafak was 10, they moved to Madrid, where she was the only Turkish pupil in the international school. As a teenager, she lived in Jordan and Germany. “Throughout all those years when I was really very lonely, books were my friends.” Shafak returned to Ankara to take a degree in international relations, followed by a PhD in political science. In her 20s, after teaching in Istanbul, she “escaped” to study in the US. Her first novel, Pinhan (The Sufi), was met with acclaim when it was published in Turkey in 1997. But her decision to write her fifth novel, The Saint of Incipient Insanities, in English was considered a betrayal by many at home.

The most significant parallel between Flaubert and Shafak is that they have both had their work put on trial: Madame Bovary for obscenity charges in 1857 and Shafak’s The Bastard of Istanbul in 2006, for “the public denigration” of Turkishness, due to her having written about the Armenian genocide. Shafak had to live with a bodyguard for a year and a half. Her picture was burned and spat on. She was acquitted, but in 2019 her novel 10 Minutes 38 Seconds in This Strange World was investigated by Turkish authorities for “crimes of obscenity” along with two earlier books, The Gaze and Three Daughters of Eve, which dealt with material such as child brides and sexual harassment. Her husband, Eyüp Can, a Turkish journalist and former editor of the Turkish liberal newspaper, Radikal, was put on a wanted list as part of President Erdoğan’s crackdown on intellectuals after the failed coup in Turkey in 2016.

She has described being a writer in Turkey as “a bit like being kissed on one cheek and slapped on the other”, with the kiss from the readers and the slap from the government. She is keen to stress how much her books are loved back home. “In countries like Turkey, a book is not a personal item. If you like a novel, you can’t just put it back on the shelf. You give it to your auntie, the auntie gives it to her neighbour. It’s incredibly heartwarming.”

But she again found herself at the centre of a storm back home after her 2017 Ted talk, titled “The revolutionary power of diverse thought”, in which she came out as bisexual. “I don’t know if it’s brave,” she says now. “I wish I could have done it before. But the abuse that I received from my own motherland for weeks uninterrupted was quite, quite bruising.”

She hasn’t been back to Turkey for 11 years. “There’s a melancholy to it. Maybe I’m in self-imposed exile,” she says. “But as a writer, I need freedom. I need the freedom of imagination, the freedom of speech. I felt like I first migrated into the English language and then into the UK. London became home. And I now feel rooted here, and I say this as someone who has led a very nomadic life.”

Her daughter and son, who have just left home for the new university term, have grown up speaking English. Her elderly mother often stays with them for long periods. “I hope I’m not offending, but I think only a few male authors above a certain age have precise writing schedules,” she says wryly. “Everyone else just juggles multiple roles.” She often writes at night, while listening to heavy metal, melodic death metal in particular, on her headphones. She plays the same song on a loop, often 80 or 90 times. She is a fan of the Armenian-American band System of a Down, who have also been very vocal about the Armenian genocide. “I love it. It gives me such energy,” she says. And somehow this makes her fiction “calmer”.

But it doesn’t make her calm. Writing doesn’t come any easier as you get older, she says. “It doesn’t matter whether it’s your first book, fifth book, tenth book, you suffer. You sit at your desk and there’s a lot of self-doubt. There’s a lot of anxiety, panic attacks. That, too, is part of the creative process.” When she is finished, she is not filled with satisfaction or pride, but grief. “I feel a sense of loss,” she says. “I find it so difficult to let go of the characters.”

Then she goes back out into the world. She thinks it is really important for women to have a voice in public life, and surprises herself by how much she loves literary festivals. “I really am an introvert by nature, so my natural habitat is just a small room full of books,” she says. “But when I’m on stage doing a literary event, it is not a chore. It’s not a burden. It is an immense treat for the mind or the soul.” As someone for whom speaking out has led to threats of imprisonment, she is frustrated by the cynicism towards intellectualism in the UK and the US. “It’s regarded as a sign of arrogance, hubris,” she says. “I’m not claiming to be an intellectual. What I am claiming is I have a lot of respect for the intellect.”

For Shafak, literature is “one of our last remaining democratic spaces where we’re not rushing from one thing to the next, we’re not just being fed snippets of information, but we slow down and we listen to each other again,” she says. “The ancient art of storytelling is so universal. It’s so timeless. It really doesn’t belong to a single ethnicity, region or religion. It belongs to all humanity. When I’m writing and in my books, I try to remember that kind of … ” For a moment she is lost for words. “I don’t know what to call it other than shared humanity.”

entries.title: John Green: ‘I devoured the Sweet Valley High books in the 1980s’
entries.summary: The American author on being inspired by Kurt Vonnegut, coming late to Jane Austen, and the brilliance of Robert Penn WarrenMy earliest reading memory I remember learning to read with dull stories about Jane going up a hill, but my earliest thrilling reading memories are of series like The Baby-Sitters Club and Sweet Valley High. In the highly gendered reading days of the 1980s, I knew those books
entries.content:
My earliest reading memory

I remember learning to read with dull stories about Jane going up a hill, but my earliest thrilling reading memories are of series like The Baby-Sitters Club and Sweet Valley High. In the highly gendered reading days of the 1980s, I knew those books were for girls, but I  devoured them.

My favourite book growing up

Besides the girls of The Baby-Sitters Club, I loved books about survival and perseverance, especially Gary Paulsen’s The Island, in which a boy discovers a secluded island and ventures there to learn about the natural world.

The book that changed me as a teenager

When I was 16, I read Toni Morrison for the first time: The Bluest Eye and Sula and Song of Solomon in quick succession. Literature had always felt a little distant (and maybe even slightly dead) to me, but Morrison helped me see that books were vital and present. I’d always known that they could transport me, but Morrison showed me that books could also transform me.

The writer who changed my mind

As a young person, the novelist Kurt Vonnegut had an outsize role in developing my values and beliefs. His fundamental humanism – his belief that humans might not yet be good news but still might be good news – inspired me then and inspires me still.

The book that made me want to be a writer

Reading Michael Chabon’s The Mysteries of Pittsburgh made me want to write books. I’d never encountered a novel before with queer main characters or such a vibrant sense of contemporary youth, and this one made me want to tell similar stories.

The book I came back to

When I was in high school, I found Holden Caulfield in JD Salinger’s The Catcher in the Rye annoying and whiny. I enjoyed the book but thought Holden just needed to snap out of it and realise how lucky he was to be a rich kid in New York City. Revisiting the story years later, it shattered me. The sadness of that novel, and the vulnerability of Holden, only became clear to me in adulthood.

The book I reread

I’ve just reread Lily King’s Heart the Lover and enjoyed it even more the second time around. I reread quite a lot, because I am fascinated by how different a great book is each time you return to it. The text hasn’t changed, of course, but I have.

The book I could never read again

I don’t feel an urgent need to return to the works of Ayn Rand, whose flimsy plots only serve to reinforce flawed ideas about how humans organise themselves and cooperate.

The book I discovered later in life

I didn’t read Jane Austen’s Pride and Prejudice until I was an adult! How I wish I could have met Lizzy Bennet when I was younger, but even so, I love that book and return to it often.

The book I am currently reading

It’s about astrophysics, called How to Build a Universe, by Dr Katie Mack. I’m anxious for anything that can help me zoom out – in this case way, way out – to understand that mine is not the only life (and, indeed, my galaxy is not the only galaxy).

My comfort read

When I need to be reminded of why I love reading and what it is about language that lights me up, I go back to All the King’s Men by Robert Penn Warren, a brilliant novel about US politics and the south but most of all about the inexorable march of time.

entries.title: ‘I know I can do anything’: new archive of AS Byatt’s papers looks inside the writer’s extraordinary mind
entries.summary: The Booker-wining author of Possession was known for her voracious research. Now, 68 boxes of her notebooks, letters and diaries acquired by the British Library reveal how she assembled the raw material of her fictionAt 20, Antonia Susan Byatt was not yet sure she could write. “Do I take myself seriously as a writer?” she asked herself in her diary in September 1956. “No, I think not.”The young By
entries.content:
At 20, Antonia Susan Byatt was not yet sure she could write. “Do I take myself seriously as a writer?” she asked herself in her diary in September 1956. “No, I think not.”

The young Byatt – who would go on to become one of Britain’s most celebrated writers, best known for her 1990 novel Possession: A Romance – was troubled by the possibility that her mind might not be equal to her ambitions. Yet her determination was already evident. On her 20th birthday, she wrote: “Today, I know I can do anything. But not yet.”

These intimate reflections can be found among the material in a major new archive of Byatt’s work, acquired by the British Library. It offers an insight into the development of the Booker prize-winning writer, who died aged 87 in 2023, and whose intricate, intellectually ambitious fiction earned her international acclaim.

The collection comprises 68 boxes of working notebooks, manuscripts, correspondence, personal diaries and documents from Byatt’s early life. It includes handwritten drafts of Possession, which won the 1990 Booker prize, and material relating to her 1978 novel The Virgin in the Garden and The Children’s Book, which was shortlisted for the Booker prize in 2009. According to the British Library’s curators, it is one of the most significant contemporary literary acquisitions the library has made in recent years.

“It’s the other side of the tapestry,” says Jenny Uglow, Byatt’s editor, who worked closely with her on Possession. “In her books, you have these extremely elaborate plots, very complicated characters with their extraordinary names. And then when you actually look behind it, there are hundreds, thousands of little threads.”

Born in Sheffield in 1936, Byatt studied English at Cambridge before continuing her education at Bryn Mawr College, Philadelphia, and at Oxford. She spent more than two decades teaching in universities and art schools, before leaving academia in 1983 to write full-time. She was known for her voracious research and her ability to weave apparently disparate fields of knowledge into her fiction. The archive allows researchers to follow Byatt as she assembles the raw material of her fiction, tests ideas and repeatedly questions whether they will work.

The documents “reveal the way her mind works”, Uglow says. “She thought extremely fast and she had one of those racing minds, almost like a three o’clock in the morning mind, everything whirling around. She’ll say things like: ‘This is fascinating, but it doesn’t fit. I can’t go on, this is not working out.’

“She got very cross if she was interrupted, or had to travel or wasn’t feeling well,” Uglow adds. “I think what the archive does is allow you to follow an extremely distinctive writer in the way that they create their work.”

The handwritten drafts of Possession are particularly illuminating. The novel, which interweaves the story of two contemporary academics investigating the lives of fictional Victorian poets, is a feat of elaborate plotting. The hundreds of pages of notebooks drafting the book show Byatt diligently working through questions of chronology and the relationships between the characters before the narrative took its final shape.

“Once she had decided on a book, it would take two, three or four years [to write it],” Uglow says. “She worked everything out scene by scene before she wrote the scene itself. She would really think it through, so when you get to the manuscript there aren’t many corrections.”

Byatt continued to write by hand well into the 2000s and 2010s. “It’s rather like craft work,” Uglow says. “There’s a connection between the brain, the imagination and the hand.”

The diaries show that Byatt’s intellectual confidence coexisted with flecks of self-doubt. At a young age, she described herself as an “intellectually slow developer” and wondered whether she had a “second rate mind”.

In another entry, she wondered whether her abstract way of thinking would prevent her from creating convincing characters – “characters with blood in them”.

The collection also contains correspondence with other writers, including the novelist Iris Murdoch, with whom Byatt had a friendly relationship, and letters documenting her exchanges with younger writers.

“If she saw a promising young writer, she was excited,” Uglow says. “She took great pleasure in seeing their books come out, and was loyal to them.”

The papers also capture Byatt’s wry observations of the people she encountered. During her time in the United States as a young woman, she offered a tart assessment of the women around her. “American women – curiously, stuntedly efficient & childlike,” she wrote. “Most of these are 26, 27 – one would imagine them less. Friendly though, and not unintelligent.”

The library estimates that cataloguing the 68 boxes will take up to two years. Once complete, the archive will sit alongside its holdings of the literary papers of writers including Angela Carter, Beryl Bainbridge, Hanif Kureishi and Graham Swift.

“The British Library is thrilled to have acquired the archive of AS Byatt,” says Helen Melody, the library’s lead curator of contemporary literary and creative archives. “Byatt sits at the heart of the British literary establishment and her prominence within postwar British literature cannot be overstated. This collection will be a hugely significant resource for researchers seeking to learn more about her life and work.”

Uglow thinks Byatt would have welcomed the acquisition. “I think she would be very happy to see her work taken seriously,” she said. “And she would have enjoyed the fact that people wanted to see it and that it was being looked after so carefully.”

entries.title: The best recent crime and thrillers – review roundup
entries.summary: The Heights by Ian Rankin; The Mortons by Scott Westerfeld and Justine Larbalestier; Murder Most Cryptic by Alys Cummings; The Deadly Inheritance of Everest Macdonald by AJ West; Inheritance by Gillian SlovoThe Heights by Ian Rankin (Orion, £25) Luxury tower blocks, those potent symbols of hyper-gentrification, the increasing wealth gap and the displacement of existing communities, are a gift to n
entries.content:
The Heights by Ian Rankin (Orion, £25)

Luxury tower blocks, those potent symbols of hyper-gentrification, the increasing wealth gap and the displacement of existing communities, are a gift to novelists. Rankin’s first standalone thriller in almost two decades centres on The Heights, 18 storeys high and facing London’s Hyde Park, where DS Gillian Gish is investigating the suspicious death of night-shift security guard Dwayne Hogarth. The high-net-worth individuals who live there, including a young singer, a gangster’s wife, a man who “made a mint in post-glasnost Russia” and the daughter of a very well-connected Zimbabwean, are either uncontactable or tight-lipped, and it soon becomes clear that the developer, despite his bravado, is in financial trouble. Everyone, it appears, has something to hide – and then a second corpse is discovered. Rankin is a superb storyteller, and this is well up to his usual high standard, while DS Gish – less complex, but considerably more relatable than John Rebus – is worthy of her own series.

The Mortons by Scott Westerfeld & Justine Larbalestier (Viking, £18.99)

There are shades of both The Sopranos and Wednesday Addams in this tale of a powerful old American family whose trade is murder, blackmail and financial fraud. As the Mortons’ great hope, Jessica, puts it, “Give your child a strong hand, a sharp knife, and a big family, then teach them loyalty without care.” The children are given pet rabbits on which to prove their lack of compassion; the family are as ruthless with their own as with everyone else, their graveyard being full of youngsters who failed to make the grade. Jessica, who achieved her first kill aged 20, looks set to take on the murderous mantle, but a summer internship leads to a train of events that culminate in the discovery of a conscience. The Mortons is vivid and exciting, with a nice vein of mordant humour, but there’s a lot of world-building to get through, some of it lacking in internal logic; it’s hard to keep track of the many characters, and the violence towards innocent people and animals may leave some readers feeling queasy.

Murder Most Cryptic by Alys Cummings (Michael Joseph, £16.99)

Cummings’s entertaining debut begins with a man walking into a meeting of people in recovery, announcing that his name is Laurence and he’s an alcoholic, then dropping dead. The group, who spot a handwritten cryptic crossword clue that’s fallen out of Laurence’s pocket – answer: Murder – are quicker to suspect foul play than the police, and when the same clue appears in the following day’s newspaper, they decide to figure out what’s going on. Told from the points of view of people trying, with varying degrees of success, to remain sober, this book involves a fair amount of unreliable narration – not least because of the memory gaps of the blackout drunk. The emergence of pertinent backstories lends rather more emotional depth than is found in the average cosy, while the discovery of further cryptic crossword clues provides an ingenious puzzle element (answers given at the end for non-cruciverbalists).

The Deadly Inheritance of Everest Macdonald by AJ West (Orenda, £20)

West’s latest historical mystery is a re-imagining of real events: actor William Terris was stabbed to death outside London’s Adelphi theatre in 1897 by deranged and destitute fellow performer Richard Archer Prince, who was subsequently found “criminally insane” and sent to Broadmoor. The action here takes place in 1917, against the backdrop of the first world war, as Everest Macdonald’s father, brother of William, hands her a packet of papers and charges her with finding out the truth about her uncle’s death. What follows is a fascinating journey that takes us back to the Indian sepoy rebellion of 1857 and encompasses “blackmail in all directions, secret love affairs, loyalties, vendettas, even phantoms and tribal curses”, as well as a plethora of hysterical thespians including real-life stars of the turn-of-the-century British stage such as Herbert Beerbohm Tree and Seymour Hicks. Well-researched, atmospheric and suitably melodramatic, this is a rip-roaring read-at-one-sitting historical mystery.

Inheritance by Gillian Slovo (Peepal Tree, £12.99)

The eponymous inheritance of Slovo’s latest novel involves political and financial corruption in a South Africa still emerging from the long shadows cast by apartheid. Novelist Deborah Harrison’s younger sister Gail killed herself after denouncing Deborah’s latest book – a re-imagining of the family tragedy that blighted their childhood – as a misrepresentation. Deborah has always accepted the official version of events, that her mother killed her father in 1984 and went to prison for it, but Gail, whose adulthood was blighted by addiction issues and escalating paranoia, maintained that this was not the case. Now she has left a will tasking her sister with finding their now-released mother, with whom they have had no contact for over 40 years, and Deborah discovers that the truth is far more complicated than she has been led to believe. This is a suspenseful and moving tale about generational trauma, the complex nature of memory, making peace and letting go.

entries.title: Make Me Well by Xand van Tulleken – an eye-opening takedown of wellness myths
entries.summary: The engaging TV doctor dismantles the spurious science behind modern day snake oils, from collagen to turmericWhen Xand van Tulleken set off on a journey into the wild west of wellness, he didn’t expect to discover anything new about vitamin D. Of all the supplements that line our shelves and social media feeds, it ought to be the least controversial; even the NHS website, which is hardly a wellsp
entries.content:
When Xand van Tulleken set off on a journey into the wild west of wellness, he didn’t expect to discover anything new about vitamin D. Of all the supplements that line our shelves and social media feeds, it ought to be the least controversial; even the NHS website, which is hardly a wellspring of quackery, advises that everyone should consider taking a daily dose during autumn and winter, when we risk becoming deficient (D is the vitamin we get mostly from sunlight, and which helps keep our bones strong).

The tiggerish TV doctor and twin brother to Chris (he’s the one who wrote Ultra-Processed People about the food industry) qualified at a time of high excitement in vitamin D circles; in the early 2000s, big studies were linking it not just to bone health but cancer, heart disease and dementia. “The range of potential problems to be solved was dizzying,” Van Tulleken writes in Make Me Well.

But – spoiler alert – it turns out evidence even of the benefits of the most medically endorsed supplement shrivels under scrutiny. After immersing himself in decades of trials and speaking to a professor who had devoted his career to what he now views as the false promise of vitamin D, Van Tulleken finds no justification for its routine consumption for all but a tiny proportion of the population who are genuinely deficient.

The vitamin D chapter follows what becomes a familiar and compelling pattern in Van Tulleken’s first proper solo book, in which he combines the rigour of an investigative journalist with medical expertise and the bouncy bedside manner that makes him such a natural broadcaster. He’s also the best kind of science writer, leaning into complexity while making it as easy to digest as a fish oil gummy (another thing you might want to stop forking out for).

As well as vitamin D, he goes deep on collagen, testosterone, multivitamins, turmeric and krill oil supplements, as well as the burgeoning markets for personalised nutrition, glucose monitoring, wearable tech and private blood screening. In each case, he finds a troubling blurring of the lines between wellness and healthcare – and yawning gaps between hype and the evidence. He also uncovers the harm that wellness fads can do to our bodies, our relationship with food and the environment.

In a chapter devoted to collagen, Van Tulleken travels to China to learn how a messy byproduct of the meat industry has been marketed as a modern elixir with a mark-up of as much as 1,000%. Ejiao, a premium kind of donkey-derived collagen, has become such a coveted source of “ingestible beauty” that manufacturers have exhausted Chinese supplies of donkey hides; soon rural communities in countries across Africa were finding that their animals were being slaughtered for export so that their skins could be boiled up and turned into expensive gummies and powders.

He also explores the history and booming business of supplements, from the literal snake oil of the late 19th century to an unwholesome contemporary market driven by podcasts, influencers and a scientific publishing industry that appears to have striking deficiencies of its own: “The more research I do, the more I see the same patterns repeatedly: conflicts of interest, industry-funded trials, industry-­owned journals and an entire system designed to exploit people.”

He concludes that, for the generally healthy person, wellness requires things that it’s hard to package and sell to supermarkets or via a subscription: a diet rich in whole foods and fruit and vegetables, for example, and a hobby that involves the achievable yet challenging mastery of some kind of rewarding skill. (The scientific evidence for the health benefits of, say, becoming a potter or learning the piano is far more robust than that for knocking back testosterone or vitamin D.)

“The right people to make you well won’t be health gurus,” Van Tulleken says at the end of a book that deserves to prompt some kind of industry reckoning. “They might be dance instructors or librarians or martial arts teachers or the person who runs your local choir.” While I consider resuming reacquainting myself with my own piano, I have no plans to dust off my bottle of vitamin D pills as the nights draw in.

entries.title: Lee Child backs launch of reading scheme to send prisons half a million books
entries.summary: The Jack Reacher author, the UK’s first prison reading laureate, said drive to improve literacy skills was a practical way to address reoffending and support rehabilitationNearly half a million books will be distributed across prisons in England, Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland this autumn, in a campaign backed by bestselling thriller writer Lee Child.The initiative, delivered by the Reading
entries.content:
Nearly half a million books will be distributed across prisons in England, Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland this autumn, in a campaign backed by bestselling thriller writer Lee Child.

The initiative, delivered by the Reading Agency charity as part of its Quick Reads programme, will see copies of 11 short books distributed, with titles selected with input from prisoners as well as staff. A book will be distributed to every cell across the prison estate, as well as stock sent to prison libraries.

Child, the UK’s first prison reading laureate, said the initiative was intended to address the “revolving door” – people leaving prison but struggling to cope outside and returning to custody.

“If we can stop one in 10 of those people from coming back, that would be a major achievement,” he said. “It would be good for society as a whole, not just for that individual prisoner and their future employer.”

Ministry of Justice statistics for 2024-25 show that 65% of initial-assessment results across public prisons in England, based on tests taken when people entered custody, were at entry levels 1-3, below the standard expected of a typical GCSE student.

Child said people who wanted to turn their lives around after prison could face compounded barriers if they had difficulty reading. “The obvious beneficiary will be somebody who is [in prison] due to some kind of mistake or unfortunate circumstance that they regret, and who wants to go straight afterwards and never come back,” he said. “But they face the problem of finding a job if they’ve got a conviction, and on top of that, if they’ve got poor literacy skills.”

Everyday tasks could also become obstacles, he said. “You can’t read a lease if you want to rent a flat; you can’t deal with utilities or a TV licence if you can’t read the official notices.”

The Quick Reads collection spans crime and thrillers, memoir, wellbeing, and a creative writing guide. Fiction titles include High Heat by Child himself; Cell One, a Lagos-set thriller by Leye Adenle; and Darkness Rising, from Bradford-based crime writer AA Dhand’s Harry Virdee series. Other books include Lemn Sissay’s memoir My Name Is Why, Andy McNab’s Today Everything Changes and Dr Alex George’s The Mind Manual. Authors featured also include Dreda Say Mitchell, Fiona Cummins, Cathy Rentzenbrink and Alex Wheatle.

Child, who has made between 30 and 40 prison visits since beginning his work as laureate last year, said one of the most common explanations he heard from people who did not read was that the books they had been given at school were boring. Quick Reads, he said, offers an alternative. “They are proper books, proper storytellers, and there’s nothing simple or childish about them, they’re just short.”

He added that improving access to books should be understood not as a soft approach to criminal justice but as a practical way to support rehabilitation and reduce reoffending. “The problem with public reaction to this kind of thing is a rather kneejerk reaction of ‘soft on crime’,” he said. “My point is that no, it’s actually hard on crime. It is focusing on where the budget and attention should really be.”

Alongside distributing the books, the Reading Agency will organise author-led workshops, creative writing activities, content for National Prison Radio and resources for prison libraries, education teams and peer supporters. The initiative is funded by the Henry Smith Foundation, a poverty-focused non-profit.

AA Dhand, whose Darkness Rising is among the selected books, said: “Books should be accessible to everyone, regardless of their circumstances or their previous relationship with reading.”

Dhand added: “In prison, reading can provide far more than temporary escape. It can build confidence, create empathy and give people the opportunity to see the world and themselves differently. If the right book reaches the right person at the right moment, it can open a door that may otherwise have remained closed.”

Karen Napier, chief executive of the Reading Agency, said the programme was built with the intention of giving people in prison choice over what they read.

“When we put a book directly into someone’s hands, we are offering more than words on a page,” she said. “Reading can offer escape, connection and space for reflection, while supporting wellbeing, confidence and learning. We want as many people as possible to have the opportunity to find a book that grabs them and discover where reading might take them.”

entries.title: Sally Rooney’s stand on Palestine is brave and humane
entries.summary: The Normal People author’s determination to support Palestine Action, even if it means that her books are withdrawn from sale in the UK, makes a mockery of Britain’s terrorism lawsIt’s hard to think of a published author in living memory who risked arrest in the UK for their political beliefs, hard to think of one whose books could be published anywhere but here. Sally Rooney went into this debacl
entries.content:
It’s hard to think of a published author in living memory who risked arrest in the UK for their political beliefs, hard to think of one whose books could be published anywhere but here. Sally Rooney went into this debacle with her eyes open: she said last July that royalties from her books, and their BBC adaptations, would be used to support Palestine Action.

Rooney’s courage is not so much in risking imprisonment, since there is a fix for that, which is what she’s doing – avoiding the UK. Rather, she has chosen the thorniest possible path for this cause. Authors can write essays and sign letters in support of the Palestinian people; actors can voice it in interviews, musicians can say it from the stage, and there is always a cost to it, whether it’s in plain sight and they’ve been kicked off a global tour, or it’s behind closed doors and they are simply excluded from opportunities. But such actions, even if they logically suggest support for a proscribed organisation, don’t entail actively breaking the terrorism laws. Rooney had taken a financial hit anyway, by pledging support for Palestine Action with her royalties; but that’s a price at least you can count. The lost sales and opportunities that ripple out from being effectively both barred from and banned in the UK are innumerable.

Yet, speaking as not-her-accountant, but as someone living in the culture she also inhabits and has made such an impact describing, the value of her stand is similarly hard to put a price on. Her authorial voice and body of work makes this intervention distinctive in its reach. She’s never been an apolitical author. Normal People was razor sharp on class, Conversations With Friends wasn’t shy of a Marxist analysis. But the work is also intimate, often domestic, I mean, the clue’s in the name – these were always normal people. It was from a reputation of delicately challenging but everyday subtlety that Rooney assumed her outrider position, and in so doing, took on the idea that caring about Gaza is somehow a crank’s life choice; insisted that it is a human response, as natural and quotidian, as passionate and important, as friendship.

It also, come on – surely at some point we’re allowed to say this – makes an absolute mockery of the terrorism legislation thus applied. Nobody anywhere thinks Sally Rooney poses a danger to the British state, or any state, just as nobody anywhere thinks a 94-year-old human rights barrister who was a friend of Ed Miliband’s late mother does. Keir Starmer, paradoxically, given that the two things in his favour were his caution and his legal hinterland, painted himself into an absurd corner, where terrorism arrests went up between 2024 and 2025 from 250 to nearly 3,000. On demos where anyone crunched the numbers, more of them were over 80 than under 20.

The history and particularity of Irish solidarity with the Palestinian cause have been discussed a lot since the painful Ed Sheeran tour, in which the singer thought a support act could be quietly ditched over a pro-Palestine song, without losing his backing band – Beoga, founder members of Irish Artists for Palestine. More broadly, Ireland has a vibrant tradition of young women with no reason to think they have the right to opine on geopolitics sticking their oar in anyway. The Dunnes Stores strike of 1984 kicked off when 21-year-old Mary Manning refused to handle some South African grapefruit, leading to her receiving only £21 a week in strike pay for two years and nine months. It reached its political crescendo less than three years later, when Ireland banned South African goods altogether in protest at apartheid. In between, though, in 1985, Desmond Tutu met Manning and her fellow strikers on his way to get the Nobel peace prize, extending as he did an invitation to visit him in South Africa – which they took him up on, only to be turned away at the border. There’s an instant echo, here, of a state showing its might at customs only to draw attention to its weakness; and of an author who, as well as that, is an ordinary citizen, whose forgone royalties are almost the least of the sacrifice, but are still a powerful emblem.

entries.title: The best books to read in October: new paperbacks from Zadie Smith, Thomas Pynchon and Francis Spufford
entries.summary: Looking for a new reading recommendation? Here are some brilliant new paperbacks, from a time-travelling fantasy novel to an eclectic essay collection. Discuss what you’re reading in paperback in the comments*** Continue reading...
entries.content:
Fiction

Fiction

Shadow Ticket

Thomas Pynchon

Everything is connected in Shadow Ticket, Thomas Pynchon’s fleet-footed noir fiction about a lindy-hopping detective in prohibition-era Wisconsin. The homemade bomb connects to the runaway cheese heiress, the cheese heiress to the federal agents, and the feds to the pro‑Nazi leagues at the bowling lanes outside town. Early-30s Milwaukee, in turn, is connected to powder-keg central Europe, where paramilitary groups have pitched camp on the Hungaro-Croatian border and guest speakers wax lyrical about “our immense fascist future”. Most likely it connects to the current moment as well, albeit wryly and slyly, with a nonchalant swing. That’s the implied final move of this merry dance of a book: the point where the past links its hands with the present.

Shadow Ticket is a Pynchon novel – the 88-year-old’s first in 12 years; his ninth overall – and so it naturally connects to the man’s back catalogue, too, and its abiding fascination with conspiracy, chaos and the churn of American pop culture. Specifically it relates back to his two previous works – Inherent Vice and Bleeding Edge – in that the story comes tailored as a dime-store whodunnit, complete with red herrings, plot twists and reams of hard-boiled dialogue. But classifications, like people, are never entirely to be trusted. Pynchon inhabits the genre like a hermit crab inside a mollusc shell, periodically peeking out from the gloom to remind us that he’s there. Xan Brooks

£9.89 (RRP £10.99) – purchase at the Guardian bookshop

Fiction

Nonesuch

Francis Spufford

Spufford’s fourth work of fiction in a genre-spanning oeuvre, Nonesuch is a historical fantasy set during the second world war, every paragraph of which is packed with authorial zest. The novel opens in London, August 1939: war has been declared, but hasn’t yet made its reality felt in the city’s streets, and Iris Hawkins, an ambitious office clerk, makes her way through the sun-baked West End in a slinky dress. One half of a disastrous date later, she’s being whisked away to a DIY surrealist film club in bohemian Bloomsbury – not her scene at all – and two extremely fateful introductions: the first to Geoffrey Hale, a sweetly apprehensive BBC television engineer; and the second to the object of Geoffrey’s guileless infatuation, one Lady Lalage Cunningham, an icy aristocratic beauty with amazing hair and worrisome political sympathies. Cue chaos. Nonesuch follows the bolshy Iris from her seedy summer’s night through a regrettable Hampstead hook-up, and, eventually, neck-deep into a time-travelling plot by “magical fascist lunatics” to assassinate Winston Churchill. The novel is a pleasing pasticcio of romance, occultism, non-Euclidean geometry and airborne adventure across the blitz-stricken rooftops of London. It is difficult to imagine it would hold together quite so well in other hands than Spufford’s. AK Blakemore

£8.99 (RRP £9.99) – purchase at the Guardian bookshop

Fiction

Beasts of the Sea

Iida Turpeinen



In November 1741 Georg Wilhelm Steller, “theologian, naturalist, and curious man”, was shipwrecked on an island between Alaska and Russia. There he found, floating in the shallow waters, a vast sirenian, Hydrodamalis gigas, nine feet long and soon to be known as Steller’s sea cow. Having made it through the winter, largely by eating the sea cows, the following August Steller and the remaining survivors of the Great Northern Expedition left the island. Within 30 years, Steller’s sea cow was hunted to extinction.

Having described these events, Finnish author Iida Turpeinen’s debut novel goes on to describe the lives of other historical figures, each of whom are touched in some way by the sea cow, now reduced to bones. There is Hampus Furuhjelm, governor of Alaska, in search of a complete skeleton, and his sister Constance, who finds peace and intellectual autonomy among her taxidermy collection. Later, there’s Hilda Olson, a scientific illustrator, and John Grönvall, specialist in the reconstruction of birds’ eggs, who is tasked with preparing a sea cow’s relics for exhibition.

Turpeinen writes in a flowing present tense, moving seamlessly from one character to another, drawing us gently but firmly onwards. Emotional detail is astutely rendered. The result is a book that is almost hypnotically readable; it’s been much garlanded in Finland and it’s easy to see why. Jessie Greengrass

£9.89 (RRP £10.99) – purchase at the Guardian bookshop

Fiction

Other People’s Fun

Harriet Lane

Ruth, the narrator of Harriet Lane’s third novel, Other People’s Fun, is corroded by envy. Alone, her marriage over, her daughter grown and her freelance work as dull as it is low paid, she is that most dangerous of characters: an overlooked middle-aged woman with nothing to lose. When she bumps into beautiful, stupid and entitled Sookie at a school reunion, she reconnects with her teenage self “and all her violent desires”. Having flown under the radar as a pupil, noticed by Sookie only because she lent her her essays, she has perfect recall of her own petty humiliations, now amplified by the fact that she can stalk her contemporaries’ “best lives” on social media, while almost none of them remember her.

The best comedy is sharpened by pain, and what Lane has pinpointed in her flint-sharp novel is something that has a highly modern resonance as the world of the haves and have-nots becomes increasingly polarised and toxic. When Ruth gets her revenge, it is as nasty as it is total. You will, I fear, howl with satisfaction. Amanda Craig

£9.89 (RRP £10.99) – purchase at the Guardian bookshop

Fiction

Absence

Issa Quincy

In Quincy’s novel, the narrator is charmed by a poem first read to him as a child by his mother, which then follows him through his life. He’s stirred by memories and emotions as he is confronted by letters and photographs, phantoms and secrets, all of which make up a life that has been affected by generations of profound familial tragedy. Quincy’s prose is deftly lyrical and imaginative; I’ve had the pleasure of hearing him read from Absence at a literary salon in London and it was entrancing. He observes the fragility of memory, and what remains after our encounters, however fleeting, with people, say a schoolteacher or an estranged aunt; you might think of him as a counterpart to the novelists Rachel Cusk and Teju Cole. Jason Okundaye

  • Absence is published by Granta

Short stories

Short stories

The Land of Sweet Forever

Harper Lee

The Land of Sweet Forever is a collection of Lee’s unpublished short stories and previously uncollected essays. However, like most such books, it has little to offer to those who aren’t diehard fans.

The short stories, written in Lee’s youth, are all badly underdeveloped. Most fail to work even as vignettes. One centres on trying to find a place to unload a truck in Manhattan; another on a temporary change to the way the doxology is sung in a Methodist church. A slender piece about the quirks of New York movie audiences is categorised as a story, but feels more like a newspaper sketch. The young Lee seems to have little sense of what a story is.

On the positive side, there is already wit and charisma in the voice. One narrator, returning to her southern home town, recognises “a tall young man whose face belonged to the Wade family, but whose body showed extensive Talbert influence. He was Talbert Wade, of course.” This may be slight, but it’s elegantly done. There are also hints of iconoclastic anger struggling to get out, especially in The Water Tower, where a 12-year-old Mississippi girl erroneously thinks she is pregnant. Understanding that being an unwed mother would wreck the lives of her whole family, she decides the only way to save them is to destroy her shameful body.

If we regard this book as literature, it is an unqualified failure. But it’s more properly seen – and will surely be read – for the light it sheds on Lee’s life. As such, it’s obliquely fascinating, largely because it radiates repression. Often there’s a sense that we’re seeing the side of Harper Lee that wasn’t exceptional, but representative of a generation of women who were mostly muzzled. Lee writes in The Cat’s Meow (perhaps the strongest story in the collection): “I suppose a lot of people like me have mastered the first lesson of living at home these days: if you don’t agree with what you hear, place your tongue between your teeth and bite hard.” We feel those painfully gritted teeth on every page of this book. In a time of rising censorship, it’s salutary to be reminded that an author as important as Harper Lee came so close to being entirely silenced. Sandra Newman

£8.99 (RRP £9.99) – purchase at the Guardian bookshop

Essays

Essays

Dead and Alive

Zadie Smith

Dead and Alive bundles various odds and ends from the past nine years: speeches, opinion pieces, criticism and eulogies for departed literary heroes – Philip Roth, Martin Amis, Hilary Mantel.

In Some Notes on Mediated Time – one of three completely new essays in the collection – Smith recalls how the “dreamy, slo-mo world” of her 1980s childhood gave way, within a generation, to the “anxious, permanent now” of social media. If you lived through that transition, you don’t have to be very old to feel ancient. When this estrangement is compounded by the ordinary anxieties of ageing, cultural commentary becomes inflected with self-pity. Smith’s identification with the protagonist of Todd Field’s Tár, a once revered conductor who finds herself shunned by the younger cohort, takes on existential proportions: “Our backs hurt, the kids don’t like Bach any more – and the seas are rising!”

Smith steers a sensible middle course on the vexed debate around “cultural appropriation” in fiction. There is more to people than their identity – “we can, sometimes, forget the mystery that lies at the heart of all selfhood”. The point is well made in a thoughtful piece on James Baldwin and the craft of writing, originally a lecture delivered to creative writing students over Zoom during the pandemic. Smith reminds her students that the essence of Baldwin’s brilliance was his ability to process politics through personal experience: he “submitted to his consciousness first and then re-examined what that might mean for his conscience”. This is sound advice, and Smith’s positions on the politics of creativity are beyond reproach, albeit commonsensical – amounting, essentially, to a caution against overcorrection and incuriosity.

When it comes to actual politics, she is less assured. Her New Yorker op-ed on the war in Gaza, published in May 2024, was widely interpreted as unhelpfully equivocal, and seemed to conflate anti-war protesters with antisemites. She has since added her signature to an open letter acknowledging Israel’s actions as genocidal. The New Yorker piece, reprinted here with a new preamble hailing the protesters as “heroic”, is an intriguing artefact: the prose is mealy mouthed, heavy on the passive voice – all the more conspicuous since Smith’s writing is normally so clear and crisp. Houman Barekat

£10.79 (RRP £11.99) – purchase at the Guardian bookshop

Memoir

Memoir

Fly, Wild Swans

Jung Chang



Remarkable success notoriously brings its own problems. Wild Swans, first published in 1991 and written by Jung Chang with the help of her husband, Irish-born historian and writer Jon Halliday, had a global impact few authors dare to dream of. It told the story of three generations of women in 20th-century China – Chang’s grandmother, her mother and herself – and became one of the most popular nonfiction books in history, selling more than 13m copies in 37 languages and collecting a fistful of awards and commendations. For any author, following that would be a challenge. Now, Fly, Wild Swans returns to the story, picking it up after Chang’s own departure from China in 1978, and revisiting episodes from the earlier work with added detail.

Few can match Chang’s ability to bring Chinese history and politics to life through deeply felt personal narrative, and few have shaped western understanding of China as broadly. Nearly 35 years on from the book that made her name, this story of suffering and success has the air of a closing chapter, a reckoning with both her achievements and the cost of the path she chose. Isabel Hilton

£9.89 (RRP £10.99) – purchase at the Guardian bookshop

Memoir

Wings

Paul McCartney

After splitting up, The Beatles faced an unprecedented challenge: how to be an ex-Beatle? McCartney yearned to play before audiences again, which he hadn’t since the Beatles stopped touring in 1966. But he couldn’t face doing it solo, the spotlight trained on him alone. So he asked Linda to help him put together a new group. This authorised, illustrated oral history, edited by cultural historian Ted Widmer, tells the story of one of the most successful bands of the 1970s – and one of the strangest.

It’s based on interviews (given for a new documentary on the band) with McCartney and former band members, as well as archive material. Widmer does an expert job of stitching this into a compelling narrative that includes cultural context – like what else was in the charts at the time – and plenty of photographs, many previously unseen. The result is a portal into a more eccentric age of pop, a fable about the tension between celebrity and creativity, and a story with elements of Spinal Tap and Wacky Races. Ian Leslie

£19.80 (RRP £22) – purchase at the Guardian bookshop
